verdict.root_cause: The only recorded change in the window is an automated environment-variable update at 05:59:13Z that set paymentservice's OTLP traces exporter endpoint — previously unset — to a loopback address (127.0.0.1:4317) inside the pod (tr_d12626f5a460). Roughly six minutes later the alert fires, and from that point paymentservice has no span-derived metric series at all: both the error numerator and the total-call denominator are absent, which is not a measured zero but a missing pipeline (tr_49317493f4cb, tr_e17e6b32c055). Meanwhile the service itself is demonstrably alive and correct: server-side Charge spans appear as children of checkoutservice calls at sub-millisecond durations (tr_387f51d86c3e), logs on both sides of the gap are clean informational charge/complete pairs (tr_4cf361da961c), and checkoutservice's aggregate error ratio is continuously sampled and flat zero straight through 06:05:15 (tr_2dc47bce9707). The most consistent reading is that the endpoint value is itself wrong — it names a local collector address that nothing in the pod is listening on — and the wrongness of that value is what breaks telemetry export, producing an observability blackout for paymentservice rather than a request-path failure. The log evidence of a hostname change across the unreturned gap (tr_4cf361da961c) means an instance replacement around 06:05 cannot be excluded, but nothing in hand attributes it to the config change or to resource pressure.
verdict.reasoning: Three independent lines converge. (1) Change: exactly one edit landed, six minutes before the alert, and it is a telemetry endpoint pointed at a loopback address whose benignity depends on a sidecar collector that no dispatch confirmed exists (tr_d12626f5a460). Code deploy, image rollout, flag flip, secret rotation and dependency bump were all explicitly ruled out on the same change log, which removes bad_deploy as a candidate. (2) Metrics: two separate paymentservice metric dispatches returned no matching series whatsoever, and both specialists noted that a healthy service still emits a total-calls denominator — so this is a broken or misrouted telemetry path, not a health reading (tr_49317493f4cb, tr_e17e6b32c055). That absence is exactly the shape a failed OTLP export produces downstream of span metrics. (3) Request path: the service is not actually failing. Traces show paymentservice serving Charge calls sub-millisecond with no error rows (tr_387f51d86c3e); logs show successful charges before and after the gap across multiple cards (tr_4cf361da961c); and checkoutservice, the immediate caller, records zero errors across 44 continuous samples spanning the alert minute (tr_2dc47bce9707). With no observed wait and no observed exhaustion, dependency_latency and resource_exhaustion have no positive support — the metrics specialist explicitly stated no restart, OOM, throttling or memory-ratio series were ever retrieved (tr_e17e6b32c055). What remains is a configuration value that is wrong in itself and whose wrongness is the mechanism, which is bad_config; restoring the previous endpoint (or pointing it at a collector that exists) is the fix, hence config_revert. I hold this at medium rather than high because the failure is inferred from a data absence plus a temporally adjacent change, not observed directly. The retrieved cart incidents are a live caution here: in both, a flat-zero/absent error signal on the suspect service was misread as health while the service was in fact broken. That pattern does not fit cleanly — traces and logs here give positive evidence of successful work, which cartservice did not — but it is the reason I have not closed out the possibility that something real happened inside the uncovered 06:05 window.
open_questions: No dispatch confirmed whether a collector or agent actually listens on 127.0.0.1:4317 in the paymentservice pod. The causal link from the endpoint change to the missing span metrics is inferred, not demonstrated; a single check of the pod's sidecar spec would settle or break this verdict.

What fired the alert at 06:05:15 is unidentified. No dispatch surfaced the alerting condition, and none of the returned signals (checkout errors, payment errors, payment latency) is elevated. If the alert was a request-path alert rather than a telemetry/no-data alert, this verdict is explaining the wrong symptom.
The log window is truncated precisely across 06:05:15, so the incident minute itself was never read (tr_4cf361da961c). Any error text or dependency name emitted at that moment is unknown.

The emitting hostname changed across that gap with the same pid, consistent with an instance replacement. Whether a restart occurred, and if so whether it was caused by the config change, an OOM kill, or an unrelated scheduling event, is entirely unmeasured — no container restart, OOM or saturation series was ever queried (tr_e17e6b32c055).

The trace result carries no per-span timestamps and is truncated, so it cannot show whether span export continued, thinned, or stopped after 05:59:13Z (tr_387f51d86c3e). A re-query split into pre- and post-05:59:13 windows would directly test the export-failure hypothesis and is the single highest-value next step.

Latency was never measured on either side: no percentile data for paymentservice (tr_49317493f4cb) and none for checkoutservice→paymentservice calls (tr_2dc47bce9707). If the exporter blocks rather than fails fast, a latency mechanism would be in play and the class could shift toward dependency_latency.

checkoutservice's error ratio carries no peer dimension, so paymentservice-specific call outcomes are not directly measured there (tr_2dc47bce9707); a per-peer breakdown would be needed to fully exclude partial downstream failure.
Triage reported 3 services and 2 unmeasured edges crossed, but only paymentservice and checkoutservice were dispatched. The third service and both unmeasured edges were never examined.
